links.note: 91 defines இன்சொல் as words mixed with tenderness (ஈரம் அளைஇ) and free of deceit (படிறு இலவாம்). 911 describes pleasant words from women who desire wealth and not from love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்), and says they bring harm (இழுக்குத் தரும்). Read together, the chapter on sweet speech already carries the condition that 911 shows failing: pleasantness of sound without love behind it is not what 91 praises.

911 warns that the இன்சொல் of women who want a man's wealth brings him harm. In 1258 a woman calls the soft speech (பணிமொழி) of her lover, a 'thief of many deceptions' (பன்மாயக் கள்வன்), the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve (பெண்மை உடைக்கும் படை). Both treat gentle words as an instrument that undoes the hearer, though 1258 is a lover's complaint in the Book of Love, not a warning the book gives in its own voice.

912 tells a man to keep away from women who weigh the gain (பயன்தூக்கி) before speaking of their good nature. 813 sets friends who weigh what they will get (உறுவது சீர்தூக்கும் நட்பு) beside 'those who take what they receive' (பெறுவது கொள்வார்), whom Parimelazhagar reads as prostitutes, and thieves, calling all three alike (நேர்). The same test, calculation of return in place of affection, condemns a friendship in 813 and a liaison in 912.

103 says help given by those who do not weigh the return (பயன்தூக்கார்) proves, when its worth is weighed (நயன்தூக்கின்), greater than the sea. 912 uses the same pair of words in the same order: the women weigh the gain (பயன்தூக்கி), and the man is to weigh their conduct (நயன்தூக்கி) and not join them. Weighing the return is what spoils a relationship in both verses, and weighing worth is the observer's proper response.

80 says the seat of life follows love, and that for those without it the body is bone wrapped in skin (என்புதோல் போர்த்த உடம்பு). 913 likens the false embrace (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம்) of women who want wealth to embracing an unknown corpse in a dark room (ஏதில் பிணம்). 913 applies 80's premise to a particular case: a body offered without love is, for the one who holds it, a dead one.

241 ranks the wealth of grace (அருட்செல்வம்) above the wealth of goods (பொருட்செல்வம்), noting that the latter is found even among the base (பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள). 914 uses the same opposition: those whose understanding examines அருட்பொருள் will not touch the poor favours of those for whom wealth itself is the thing of value (பொருட்பொருளார்). The ranking stated in the book of virtue becomes here a practical ground for refusal, and 919 goes on to name the men who do not refuse as பூரியர்.

285 says that a loving nature with grace in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's unguarded moment. 914 opposes those who examine அருட்பொருள் to women for whom பொருள் is the only thing of value. In the chapter on theft and in this one, the same pair, aiming at grace or aiming at goods, sorts people into two kinds that do not mix.

636 asks what subtle scheme can stand before those who have native acuteness together with book-learning (மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்). 915 says those whose knowledge is made excellent by goodness of intellect (மதிநலத்தின் மாண்ட அறிவினவர்) do not touch the favours of women common to all; Parimelazhagar reads this too as natural intellect perfecting acquired knowledge. The pairing shows the same compound of mind being credited in statecraft with seeing through stratagems and here with keeping a man from a private vice.

915 calls the women பொதுநலத்தார், those whose favours are common to all, and says the wise will not touch them. In 1311 a wife tells her husband that all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்), calls him பரத்த, and refuses his chest. The reproach of being 'common' is turned on the man there, and it is a sulking wife's charge in the Book of Love, not a judgement the book makes itself.

149 asks who deserve good (நலக்குரியார்) and answers: those who do not touch the shoulders of a woman who belongs to another (பிறர்க்குரியாள் தோள் தோயாதார்). 916 says those who would spread their own good (தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார்) do not touch the shoulders (தோயார் ... தோள்) of women who spread their poor favours. The same phrase and the same link between abstaining and one's நலம் appear for another man's wife and for the courtesan.

57 says confinement does little to guard women, and that the guard kept by their own நிறை, firmness, is the chief one. 917 says it is men without a heart of நிறை (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace while their hearts tend other things. The same inner firmness that 57 names as a wife's real protection is here named as what a man lacks when he goes to such women.

864 says the man who does not let go of anger and has no நிறை (நிறையிலன்) is easy prey for anyone, at any time and place. 917 says those without நிறைநெஞ்சம் are the ones who go to women whose hearts are set on something else. In both the lack of self-command is what exposes a man, to enemies in 864 and to women who want what he has in 917.

918 says that for those without discerning understanding the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு, which Parimelazhagar glosses as the touch of a spirit-woman who takes life through desire. In 1082 a lover says that her returning his look is like an attacking அணங்கு (தாக்கணங்கு) arriving with an army. The same figure of the woman as an afflicting spirit is a lover's praise in the Book of Love and a warning in 918.

910 says the folly that comes of attachment to a woman never exists in those whose hearts hold deliberation (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து இடனுடையார்). 918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an affliction to those who lack examining understanding (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு). The neighbouring chapters, on subservience to a wife and on courtesans, give the same safeguard: a mind that thinks the matter through.

835 says a fool can in one birth earn the mire (அளறு) into which he will enter and sink (புக்கழுந்தும்) for seven. 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who set no limit the அளறு in which base men without worth sink (ஆழும்). The same mire, which Parimelazhagar takes as hell in both verses, is a future consequence in 835 and is identified in 919 with the pleasure itself.

920 says double-minded women, liquor and dice are the companions of those whom Fortune has removed from herself (திருநீக்கப்பட்டார்). 936 says those covered by the goddess of misfortune named gambling (சூதென்னும் முகடி) do not eat their fill and suffer. Both verses describe a vice through the two sister goddesses: in 920 the vices attend the man Tiru has already left, in 936 one of them is Mugadi herself.

920 names women of two minds (இருமனப் பெண்டிர்), which Parimelazhagar explains as a mind that joins and does not join a man at once. 974 says greatness, like women of one mind (ஒருமை மகளிர்), exists only by guarding oneself. The two phrases are opposites, and where single-mindedness is 974's model for keeping greatness, doubleness in 920 goes with dice and drink as the company of the unfortunate.

605 lists delay, forgetfulness, sloth and sleep as the pleasure-boat that those bound for ruin desire (கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்). 920 lists double-minded women, liquor and dice as the attachments of those Fortune has left. Both verses give a short list of habits and present them as what the already ruined are drawn to, as much a sign of their state as a cause of it.

653 tells those who mean to rise to leave off any deed that dims their lustre (ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை). 921 says those who live in love of liquor (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்) are never held in awe and lose their lustre (ஒளியிழப்பர்). 921 gives a named instance of the kind of act 653 warns against in general.

939 says that clothing, wealth, food, lustre (ஒளி) and learning do not come near a man who takes to gaming. 921 says those devoted to liquor lose their ஒளி and are not feared. The adjoining chapters on drink and dice both count the loss of ஒளி, the standing that makes a man regarded, among the costs.

922 forbids drinking and adds that if anyone drinks, it should be those who do not want to be counted by the worthy (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). 656 forbids any act the worthy condemn (சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை), even to relieve one's own mother's hunger. In both the judgement of the சான்றோர் is the measure of conduct; 922 states it as the price a drinker must be willing to pay.

69 says a mother rejoices more than at the birth when she hears her son called a worthy man (சான்றோன்). 923 says drunken joy is unpleasant even before the mother who bore one (ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாது), and asks what it must be before the worthy (சான்றோர் முகத்து). Both verses set the mother and the சான்றோர் side by side as the two audiences for a son's character, to opposite effect.

1047 says a man in poverty that is not joined to virtue is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும்). 923 says drunkenness is unpleasant even in his mother's presence (ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும்). Both use the mother, who Parimelazhagar notes is pleased whatever her son does, as the last person whose regard a man could lose, and say that this condition loses it.

924 says the good woman called Shame (நாண் என்னும் நல்லாள்) turns her back on those with the fault of liquor. 1040 says the good woman called Land (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள்) laughs at those who sit idle pleading poverty. The same personifying phrase makes a quality or a resource into a woman who responds to a man's conduct, by leaving in one verse and by mocking in the other.

924 says shame turns away from the drinker. In 1288 the speaker tells her lover that his chest is to her as liquor is to those who have enjoyed it, wanted even though it does harm that brings disgrace (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The simile in the Book of Love takes for granted what 924 teaches, that drink disgraces, and uses it to describe a desire that persists in spite of shame.

831 defines folly as taking hold of what harms and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). 925 says that giving wealth to get unawareness of one's own body (பொருள்கொடுத்து மெய்யறியாமை கொளல்) comes from not knowing what one is doing (கையறியாமை). Buying drink is 831's definition carried out as a single transaction: goods go out and an injury comes in.

838 says a fool getting something into his hand is like a deranged man getting drunk (மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்று). 925 says paying out wealth to buy oblivion shows ignorance. 838 uses drunkenness as the image for what a fool does with property, and 925 describes drunkenness itself as a fool's use of property.

339 says death is like falling asleep and birth like waking from sleep. 926 says sleepers are no different from the dead (துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர்), and likewise those who drink are always eating poison (நஞ்சுண்பார்). The likeness of sleep and death that 339 uses to describe the passage between lives is used in 926 as a premise: as the sleeper is for that time as good as dead, the drinker is as good as poisoned. Parimelazhagar says the shared ground is the absence of awareness.

271 says the five elements laugh inwardly (அகத்தே நகும்) at the hidden conduct of a man with a deceitful mind. 927 says those who drink and droop are seen through and always laughed at by their own town (உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர்); Parimelazhagar takes கள்ளொற்றி as drinking in concealment. In both, concealed conduct has a witness that laughs, the elements within the body in 271 and the neighbours who infer what is going on in 927.

928 tells the drinker to stop saying he has never been drunk, because what he hid in his heart shows all the more at that moment (ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்). In 1161 a woman says she would hide her pain, but like spring water for those who draw it, it increases (ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). Both end on மிகும்: the attempt to conceal an inner state is answered by its overflowing, in drink and in love.

293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn the liar afterwards. 928 concerns one such lie, 'I have never been drunk' (களித்தறியேன்), about something the speaker's heart knows, and says that drink brings the hidden thing out. 293 gives the inner penalty for this kind of lie and 928 adds an outward one, exposure.

849 says one who tries to show something to a man who does not see ends up unseeing himself, while the other goes on seeing as he saw. 929 says showing reasons to a drunk man (களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல்) is like searching with a flame for someone sunk under water. Both use காட்டு, showing, for instruction that cannot reach its hearer; 849 says it rebounds on the one who shows, 929 only that the light goes out.

190 asks what harm could come to living beings if people saw their own faults as they see those of strangers. 930 gives a case: a drinker, while sober, sees another man drunk, and the verse asks whether he does not think of the lapse of his own drinking (உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு). Parimelazhagar reads it as 'it seems he does not', which makes 930 an instance of the failure 190 describes.

539 says: when you are swelling with your own joy, think of (உள்ளுக) those who were ruined by negligence. 930 asks whether the sober drinker, seeing a drunk man, does not think of (உள்ளான்கொல்) his own slackness when drunk. Both ask a person to read his own condition in someone else's ruin, and both place the reflection at the moment when it is hardest or most needed.
